Regarding the phrase "first attained" and so forth in the superior grade [of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*], the preceding "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" states: "In the past, he was named the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana. Within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies. Later, he was reborn in that land, suddenly appearing by transformation within the house of King Śuddhaguṇa.
He said to his father: 'I have already previously attained the dhāraṇī for understanding all languages.'"

Since it is said that one "attains all languages upon changing bodies," it appears as though they are attained only after the change of body. However, if it says, "I have already attained them previously," this seems to refer to the samādhi of the physical body (rūpakāya) attained earlier; since this very samādhi is also called the dhāraṇī of language, it is therefore stated that "it is still a material phenomenon (rūpadharma)."

The phrase "it is still thus" indicates that it is the same as before; therefore, these words and the physical body (rūpakāya) differ only in terms of body and speech. How could it be that the manifested body cannot preach the Dharma? While the activities may differ, their underlying principle must be identical; thus, it is most convenient to interpret the text by using alternative names for the same reality.

This refers to the samādhi and dhāraṇī of the Perfect Gate (yuanmen). They must be identical in essence but different in name: samādhi arises from concentration (samatha), while dhāraṇī arises from wisdom (prajñā). Because they are the inconceivable union of concentration and wisdom, they can be employed interchangeably; this accords with the explanation below regarding the fulfillment of the three wheels (trimaṇḍala).
Furthermore, the classification of samādhi and dhāraṇī beneath the tongue is simply the six faculties of the true stage.

In the initial explanation of the "Universal Gate" chapter, causes and conditions and so forth were not mentioned; this is the general and specific interpretation, which fully possesses the three modes of explanation, with only the "contemplation of the mind" being absent.

Regarding the "and so forth" (*yathā*) following "wisdom and abandonment" (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) within the ten pairs: this merely provides a sequential indication and explanation, as there was no time to list them beforehand.

As for the fact that both "person" (*pudgala*) and "dharma" are stated to have "many kinds," with "and so forth" (*yathā*) annotated to each, these all indicate the one reality along with the seven expedient means, as well as persons and dharmas.
Regarding the "Question and Answer on the Prior and the Posterior": the prior question is as stated in the text.
As for the subsequent question and answer, it refers to such passages as, "How does one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "merit can transform into longevity": even Arhats are still able to redirect merit into longevity; how much more so for one who manifests through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), transforming inconceivable merit into the Wisdom of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)? This non-duality of merit and wisdom is what is termed "transformation," which serves as the analogy for the nine pairs.
Regarding the phrase "like a jewel raining down treasures": if that which is transformed results in inconceivable merit, it differs from the lower stages.
As for the "wish-fulfilling jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*), the jewel possesses manifold virtues, as detailed in the fifth fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Mohe Zhiguan*).
Regarding "digging a well" and so forth, as the *Avataṃsaka* states:

"If there is a world that is first being formed, whatever necessities for livelihood sentient beings require, the bodhisattva at that time acts as a craftsman, yet never manufactures instruments for killing."

The initial summary is as explained in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning): regarding the note "at that time" at the beginning, it refers to the four [principles], namely the four *siddhāntas*.
If one interprets the meaning of the text so as to bring it into accord with the four *siddhāntas*, [the intent is fulfilled].
Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattvas of the East," etc., a question is raised:
Why was it previously said "summon" (*śodhana*) and now said "proclaim" (*bhāṣaṇa*)?
The answer is:
In the initial invocation at the beginning of the preceding text, the term "summon" (zhào) must be used;
since this is now the conclusion of the exposition, the term "expounded" (shuō) is used.
Therefore, the end of the chapter states: "When this chapter was being expounded."
In both instances, the moment they first heard the name constitutes the "world" (loka).
In both, providing teachings according to their needs constitutes the "person" (pudgala).
In both, the means by which they attained samādhi through answering questions constitutes the "removal of doubt" (saṃśaya-vinodana).
In all cases, there are differences in the benefits gained through hearing [the Dharma], which constitute the attainment of the Way.

Regarding the term "exposing one shoulder" (*piāndǎn*) mentioned in the Sūtra: in this land, one bares the flesh of the shoulder to express repentance for transgressions, whereas in that country, one exposes the shoulder out of reverence; thus, it is simply that the customs of these two lands differ.
First, I shall explain the name "Akṣayamati. Within this, I first explain "inexhaustible" (akṣaya), initially citing three sūtras;

next, I summarize these to establish the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). First, I cite the *emptiness* (*śūnyatā*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *provisional* (*upāya*) from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, and the *middle* (*madhyama*) from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* elucidates emptiness, it is "inexhaustible";
as for the eighty inexhaustible gates in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, since they consist of many different gates, they constitute the "provisional."
In the *Vimalakīrti*, that which is "inexhaustible" (akṣaya) possesses neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; because it is the negation of both extremes, it is the Middle Way.
Next, in explaining the meaning, one first applies the three contemplations and subsequently provides a conclusion.

Although both object and cognition are cited together within the initial contemplation of emptiness, the primary point is that they are entirely devoid of self-nature when in conjunction; since cognition is empty in accordance with the object, this intent of the inexhaustible family is termed the "intent of emptiness."
Next, from "Furthermore, the mind" (*punar api citta*) onwards, it refers to the provisional person (*pudgala*): the mundane and supramundane are the objects, and wisdom follows these objects;

as the objects are manifold, so too is wisdom manifold. Next, it refers to the central [mind]: because one can contemplate the nature of the mind as being central, that which is contemplated is also central; this is explained in terms of wisdom illuminating the object.

The section beginning with "This refers to" concludes [the discussion]. Since the concluding texts for both sections equally state "contemplative wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), these all refer to the questions and answers concerning the means of establishment (*sādhana*).
As for the repeated mention of "adornment of wisdom" (*prajñā-alaṃkāra*), it indicates that the questions and answers have already completed the two types of adornment.

Now, to explain its meaning: when it is said that "question and answer" constitute adornment, this refers to the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbhāra*) among the two types of adornment—concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom.
Furthermore, both the names of the two bodhisattvas and the name of the Buddha are established based on wisdom.

Regarding the four lines beginning with “Many sufferings for one person,” in each and every line, there is suffering that all should be saved from and whose name may be upheld; because these exist as five sets and ten pairs universally, they provide benefit in every thought-moment.
It is the same for all Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching; they simply act in accordance with conditions.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says, "At that moment, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," some place the three characters "Avalokiteśvara" at the beginning of the subsequent phrase, while Master Xinghuang places them at the end of the preceding phrase and adds the three characters "Avalokiteśvara" again at the beginning of the subsequent phrase.
Neither of these two positions is correct; furthermore, there is no need to supplement the beginning of the subsequent phrase.
Someone asks: "Why is it that among those with identical mindfulness, some are subject to retrogression while others are not?"

Answer: Shared mindfulness is what manifests the capacity [for awakening]. Liberation from the obscurity of existence may be either manifest or latent; because past and present conditions differ, the benefits received have distinct grades. If one’s capacity for resonance is profound, even fixed karma can be transformed; if past and present conditions are shallow, even subtle suffering will leave no trace.
There are also those who say:
"The three calamities have both great and small forms. The great refer to fire, water, and wind; the small refer to life, body, and wealth.
Regarding the sequence of the great ones, there are two possibilities: first, from small to large, which is consistent with the meaning of time;"
Furthermore, regarding the transition from the urgent to the relaxed, this is not necessarily so; for fire does not exclusively represent urgency, nor does wind exclusively represent relaxation.
Each category also has two aspects: first, from the heavy to the light; second, from the difficult to the easy.
This may indeed be so; the details regarding these matters are fully recorded in works such as Xie Fu’s *Record of Avalokiteśvara’s Miraculous Responses*.

Regarding the "karmic conditions of the three types of action" mentioned in the separate response: the seven calamities constitute the karmic condition of speech, because one invokes the name; the three poisons constitute the karmic condition of mind, because one is made to maintain constant mindfulness; and the two kinds of seeking constitute the karmic condition of body, because one constantly performs prostrations.

Regarding "calamities of fire," some cite the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), which distinguishes seven types of fire: first, ghost-fire; second, dragon-fire; third, lightning-fire; fourth, mountain-spirit-fire; fifth, human-fire; sixth, tree-fire; and seventh, bandit-fire.
Regarding "human fire," when evil karma arises, fire spontaneously issues from one's own body.

Regarding "tree fire," it is like when trees spontaneously emit fire during a prolonged drought; yet, once water is released, these fires vanish, lacking the seven characteristics. How much more so for that which lacks the seven characteristics and has nothing with which to correspond? Therefore, they are not employed.

In the present text, both [the Lotus Sūtra and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*] contain three fires; although their names are the same, their depths differ. If this were not the case, how could the greatness of Avalokiteśvara’s power and the profundity of the merit of those who recite his name be revealed?
In the section "Entering the Mahāyāna," the following citation from the *Śāstra* provides a comparative evaluation.
Regarding the phrase "sixty-two billion" and so forth, some say:
there is no difference between the bodhisattvas; [the text] intends to emphasize Avalokiteśvara specifically.
Some say that there are two gates in the Buddha-dharma, namely the equal and the unequal.
The unequal is like the various teachings on the rituals for paying homage to the Buddhas, which differ in their specific merits.
Regarding "equality," the merit obtained is no different.
Now I ask: if all is equal, and the Buddha is neither partial nor unequal, why is it not equal?

Because the Buddha cannot possess gradations, whether things are equal or unequal is merely a matter of conditions; yet, although they are conditioned, this has not yet been fully addressed in the objection. Therefore, one must rely on the current distinction between the partial and the perfect to provide the explanation.
Not only do the various teachings for Bodhisattvas differ, but even within a single teaching, the established traces vary; this is a judgment based on the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

If one distinguishes by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the correspondence between mind and object, the present case falls under the category where both are present. In the case of those who uphold [the teachings] with sixty-two billion [beings], both mind and object are inferior; in the case of those who receive and uphold [the name of] Avalokiteśvara, both mind and object are superior. This is the contemplation according to the definitive teaching of that specific teaching.
If these two are mutually interrelated, then both the object and the mind would undergo transformation.
Question:
Why, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*, is the name of sixty-two billion Ganges-sands of Buddhas used as a standard for comparison?
Answer: Some claim that the *Śāstra* is erroneous, but we maintain that it is not so.
First, we shall set forth the text of the *Śāstra*, and second, we shall provide a brief commentary and explanation.
The *Treatise* states:
"Regarding the claim that upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara is equal in merit to upholding the names of sixty-two billion Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are two reasons:
first, because of the power of faith; second, because of ultimate knowledge."
The power of faith is further twofold:
first, seeking to become like Avalokiteśvara because of ultimate faith; second, giving rise to a mind of reverence because one thinks, "I too shall attain those same merits."

Regarding the second, ultimate knowledge: it is because one definitively knows the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The dharma-realm is termed the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), for a bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is able to realize and enter the equality-body (*samatākāya*) of all Buddhas.

The "equal body" refers to the *dharmakāya* of true suchness; therefore, upholding [the name of] Avalokiteśvara is no different from the merit of sixty-two billion Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now, based on this evidence, it should be understood that one must rely upon the "complete" (yuan) interpretation. Why is this?

Within these two meanings, the power of faith pertains to phenomena (shi), while ultimate reality pertains to principle (li); only when phenomena and principle mutually support one another can the object of mindfulness be fully established.
Within the two [sections] on the power of faith, since it says, "I seek a body like that of Avalokiteśvara," this refers to the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
Furthermore, when it says, "I shall also attain the merits of Avalokiteśvara," this refers to the saṃbhogakāya (reward body).
Only when vows and retributions are brought into alignment can one’s aspiration be fulfilled;
yet for those who simply contemplate the merit of the fruit, why must they understand the underlying principle?
Therefore, the subsequent section states, "knowing the dharma-realm," and so forth.

Next, the citation of the stage of "evidential attainment" refers to the first bhūmi; this is cited merely as a partial realization to enable people to recognize it. Therefore, one should know that if one contemplates the three bodies of Avalokiteśvara, one must instead use the contemplation of the Buddha's body as a point of comparison.
If one discusses this from the perspective of the Dharma-body, even if one were to cite all the Buddhas of the ten directions, their merit would be equal; how could it be limited to sixty-two?

Therefore, although the text of the *Śāstra* appears to quote the sūtra, it is actually an augmented sentence intended to explain the meaning—just as at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, when the Buddha wished to preach the Great Dharma, he added three phrases to provide an explanation for what was difficult to understand and difficult to know.

Regarding the passage "thirty-three bodies and nineteen sermons," one should specifically indicate the details of their combination and separation; however, because the summary mentions only a few, there are but nineteen, just as the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly are summarized as a single sermon.

Regarding the phrase "concluding the particulars and opening the general": the preceding thirty-three bodies are the particulars; therefore, it concludes by saying, "accomplishing such merits. This very sentence then serves as the opening for the subsequent general statement, which is why the following general description says, "various forms," and so forth.
Question:
This sutra reconciles the three vehicles; why then does it say that one "should [use] the three vehicles, etc."? Answer:

Since their forms differ while the Dharma is one, the "Chapter on the Exquisite Voice" states: "Through various transformations, he preaches this sutra. Those who do not perceive this mistakenly claim that the teaching of the Three Vehicles is erroneous.
Question:
Why is it that in the "Exalted Sound" (Samantamukha-parivarta) chapter, the four vehicles are placed at the end,
whereas in the "Avalokiteśvara" chapter, the three vehicles are placed at the beginning?
Furthermore, is there no bodhisattva? Answer:
Generally speaking, there is nothing that is not a bodhisattva; as for the necessity of specific manifestations, it is merely due to the brevity of the text.
Furthermore, as for the thirty-three bodies, they respond immediately according to what is perceived; how could there be any sequence of before and after?
It is simply that the two texts mutually clarify their distinctness.

Regarding the phrase "the text is broad while the meaning is narrow" up to "and so forth": it is called "broad in text" because it opens up many phrases, and it is called "narrow in meaning" because the intent refers only to the manifest text.
Regarding the phrase "the summary answer is concise," it consists of only twelve characters.
As for the statement "the meaning is vast," since it mentions "various kinds" (*nānāvidha*), what could it possibly not encompass?
Regarding the "merits of the Chapter on Hearing" and the phrase "upholding the earth," the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:

"A bodhisattva possesses ten qualities that are called the 'Earth-Holding Samādhi. Just as the earth of the world: first, it is vast; second, it is the support for sentient beings; third, it is without preference for the good or bad; fourth, it receives great rains; fifth, it produces grasses and trees; sixth, it is the basis for seeds; seventh, it produces various jewels; eighth, it produces various medicinal herbs; ninth, it is unmoved by the wind; and tenth, it cannot be startled even by the lion's roar."
"The Bodhisattva is also like this.
Each [section] of the sutra corresponds accordingly.
Now, it is said that only by judging through the eight teachings can one properly apply them to the present sutra.

Regarding the phrase "the merits of the 'Chapter on Hearing,' etc. below: one should contrast various sūtras with the present treatise to distinguish between their common and specific benefits, thereby determining the differences in their pedagogical characteristics, such as whether they are mutually inclusive or otherwise. If a teaching were exclusively Hinayāna and exoteric, it would ultimately never result in the attainment of Mahāyāna benefits; yet, if a teaching secretly yields Mahāyāna benefits, it cannot be openly transmitted. Although such a teaching may not be transmitted, its underlying intent must still be discerned.

If, as in the case of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā and similar classes of scripture, the benefit derived from hearing is common because the sections are shared, then these possess both the exoteric and esoteric and are indeterminate; those who know each other [of the teachings] are said to be "indeterminate," while those who do not know each other are said to be "secret."
Thus, within a given section or chapter, some may resemble the Great [Vehicle], yet their benefit may be either great or small;
some may resemble the Small [Vehicle], yet their benefit may likewise be great or small; and some may encompass both the Great and the Small, with their benefit also being great or small.
All of these are resolved by means of the three meanings previously discussed; one must reflect upon them!
Reflect upon them!

This present sutra is exclusively Great (Mahāyāna), and within the Great, it is exclusively Perfect (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra). It contains no esoteric, partial, or inferior teachings; therefore, from beginning to end, there is no partiality in its exposition of the chapters.
Although within the Perfect [Teaching] there are also instances of the non-retrogressive resolve and the realization of non-arising, these are not shared with the partial or Hinayana teachings;
it is precisely for this reason that the benefits are distinguished according to the respective divisions.

Therefore, although the "Chapter on King Yan" states that "the Dharma-eye has the same name but different substance," it certainly does not refer to the first fruit; it must be judged as the stage of the Dharma-eye of the six faculties' purity, which corresponds to the seventh level of faith and above.
If hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* were to cause one to attain the first fruit [of the path], then the textual meaning of the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would be undermined.

Regarding the statement, "The 'first one' is a horizontal explanation" (*heng-shi*), this concludes the three preceding layers of explanation on the "unequaled with the unequaled" (*wu deng-deng*) to establish it as the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

When the single thought-moment of the Buddha-realm is viewed in relation to the principle, it is called "horizontal" (*heng*); because the Buddha-mind and the principle are equal in both meanings, it is termed "horizontal.
Next, when the initial mind takes the ultimate principle as its object, the contrast between the beginning and the end constitutes "vertical" (*shu*).
Regarding the third meaning: when the mind and principle are in profound accord as a single entity, both are ineffable; who then could discuss their horizontal or vertical dimensions?
The first explanation—that it is "only the Buddha"—means that the mind is itself emptiness.
Next, the commentary explains the universal applicability of conventional designations.
Third, it clarifies that neither of the two aforementioned [extremes] can be apprehended.

The verses at the end of the text were not translated by Master Kumārajīva; recent scholars all claim they exist in the Sanskrit original, yet this too leaves unexamined the profound intent of Master Kumārajīva.
The *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:

"The verse was translated by Jñānagupta. Since we follow the old edition here, there is no further commentary; it is attributed to the original author as recorded in detail in the eighth fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
In the "Explanation of the Dhāraṇī Chapter," regarding the phrase "its four" appearing twice below the heading "Dhāraṇī," both instances refer to the four *siddhis*.

First, it concerns the translation of the name; second, from "various masters" onwards, it concerns the explanation of the meaning; third, from "in the evil age" onwards, it summarizes these two layers to clarify the underlying purpose.
The first section also has two parts:

first, the primary exposition based on the four *siddhāntas*; second, the clarification of the four *siddhāntas* by contrasting them with the permissions and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) found in various sutras.
Regarding the first passage: because good and evil differ, this corresponds to the *loka-siddhānta*.

Next, because the first category possesses both [aspects], it is annotated as "its second and third": being able to uphold the side of goodness constitutes the human [vehicle]; being able to obstruct the side of evil constitutes the remedial [vehicle]; and the central goodness constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the two characters "zhēchí" (prohibiting and upholding) fully embody the four *siddhāntas*.
Master Sheng said:
"Because those with shallow understanding and weak resolve for upholding the teachings are close to [delusion], they are encouraged by means of incantations."
The commentary states:
"Because the hidden and the manifest provide mutual assistance, it is called *dhāraṇī*.
Master Daosheng’s [interpretation] is far removed from this commentary."

The original purpose was to protect those who propagate the sutras from difficulties; how could it be that this is merely a forceful urging toward incantations, entirely vulgarizing and distorting worldly customs? As stated by the Buddha when Bhaiṣajyarāja offered [his head] to sixty-two billion Buddhas, and as stated by the Buddha when Vīradatta [offered his head] to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—let alone the fact that the Four Guardian Kings and the Seven Rākṣasī Sisters all requested and received the Buddha’s seal of approval to protect the Dharma—how can one say this is merely a forceful urging toward incantations?

However, as for the meaning of "dhāraṇī" (zhòu), it fundamentally should not be translated [into Chinese]. As stated in the "Exhortation to Resolve" (Quàn fā): "When a bodhisattva hears this, they should know it to be the supernatural power of Samantabhadra. How could this be the same as [mundane] arts?
If it were entirely impossible to translate, why did Zhu Fahu translate it?
If he did not understand the reason for not translating it, why would one doubt his rearrangement of the chapters?

Regarding the three terms such as "Great Illumination" (*Daming*), they are, when discussed generally, simply *prajñā*. Because *prajñā* subsumes everything, it is called a *dhāraṇī*; because it universally upholds, universally maintains, universally destroys, and universally pacifies, it may all be termed a *dhāraṇī*. This can be understood by reflecting upon them individually in relation to the three teachings.
Thus, these general and specific [mantras] are further termed "general.
The specific ones are those found in the present sutra for the purpose of protecting the Dharma.

Other sutras vary according to their specific functions—whether for averting calamities, increasing prosperity, or summoning—and each of those texts also possesses its own distinct visualization methods (*dhyāna*). This is why the new translations uniformly designate them as *mantra* (true words) or *vidyā* (wisdom/incantations). When the ancients saw that the secret [teachings] were not translated, they treated them as analogous to the indigenous Chinese methods of prohibitions and incantations, and consequently rendered them using the term "incantation" (*zhòu*).
What is now stated are all the seed-syllables of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable secret mantras.
The notation "and so forth" (yún yún) indicates that their meaning should be explained as was briefly understood above.

Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the mantra following the section on "the various masters": as for the first passage, because the names of the kings differ, evil is quelled and goodness is produced.

As for the subsequent passage, it employs "correspondence" (yoga) to signify the production of goodness; although there are words concerning the punishment of offenses, they serve strictly to ensure compliance with the teachings.
Regarding the third passage, "secret treatment" (*mi-dhi*) refers to the application of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

The fourth passage has three parts: first, it clarifies the intent of the mantra; second, it cites a specific case to explain and establish its validity; third, from the words "the mantra is also like this," it reiterates and concludes the preceding points. By being fully endowed with these four dharmas, one accomplishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); thus, the secret [mantra] being endowed with these four is what is meant by "conforming to principle."

First, regarding the "world where illness is cured": it refers to the removal of transgressions through their remedies, the cultivation of goodness for the sake of humanity, and the alignment with the Way according to the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
From the section on the "evil world" downward, the underlying intent can be understood.

Thus we know that this differs fundamentally from Master Daosheng’s [view]. The commentators refer to it as a "Praise" (*zan*), yet as it does not diminish the Great Dignity (*dayi*), it ultimately does not equal the work of Dharmarakṣa.
Regarding the "Chapter on the King of Adornment," the statement that its "causal conditions originate from other sūtras" has not been verified.

This passage also possesses the four *siddhāntas*: the first is the *loka-siddhānta*; from "Furthermore, adorning... onwards is the *puruṣa-kāra-siddhānta*; from "This king... onwards, which subdues the evils of the various faculties, is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and from "Although born... onwards is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Regarding the first passage: "Guǐ" (晷) is pronounced "guǐ" and refers to the movement of the sun and moon.
"Kè" (刻) refers to the *lòukè* (leak-drops), meaning the divisions of time.

"Kākā" (喀喀) is the sound of spitting; it describes the appearance of one who does not advance. The intended meaning is that failing to take even a single meal obstructs a long journey by ten thousand *lǐ*; if a *xún* (ten days) consists of only nine meals, it further hinders one's lofty ambition.
The white curl radiates light toward the east, illuminating Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound).
This serves two purposes: first, to demonstrate the benefits of extensively propagating the sutra so as to encourage the disciples who receive the Dharma;

second, to show that the assembly is not in vain. Thus, the *Sutra* refers to "Lady Jingde" as the Bodhisattva Zhuangyanxiang (Adorned Appearance), who is now present before the Buddha and is none other than Miaoyin.

Regarding the "Scripture on Protection by Divine Mantras," let us speak of it last; according to the preceding [pattern], one should also say: "Practicing asceticism, protecting the Dharma through divine mantras, and propagating the sutras. By manifesting his body to preach the Dharma, he established dual standards for both master and disciple. Thus, those who were enlightened and reached the East did so because they recognized the merit of coming and going.

Before arriving, he first said, "I wish to see the Medicine King," and so forth; furthermore, Flower Virtue was escorted by Wondrous Sound, along with the assembly initiated in this land. Since the Medicine King is the master of the dhāraṇīs, they together accomplish the transformation of the two sons. Moreover, this serves to connect the past and present so that those in the current assembly may simultaneously recognize them, realizing that their past causes have not been lost and that the merit of the traces of transformation is profound. Thus one knows that skillful means are unfathomable and that the seeds planted in the distant past are difficult to extinguish.

Regarding the phrase "explaining the prior conditions for the four noble ones": because these prior conditions differ, the attainment of sainthood occurs sooner or later; thus, one distinguishes between the agent and the object, and only then does one reform their errors.

Furthermore, since the means of benefiting sentient beings are manifold and the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox diverge, once those to be transformed have become proficient, the transformer may then set aside their heterodox methods.

Now, judging from the manifested traces and the subsequent explanations, at the time this transformation was established, there was one ordinary person and three sages. However, if we follow the Buddha’s own words, “In order to guide King Subhavyūha and all sentient beings, I have preached this Lotus Sutra,” and considering that the eighty-four thousand members of the royal palace were all capable of receiving and upholding it, while the two sons and forty-two thousand others all arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, then the king and all those who underwent the transformation were merely provisional manifestations.

Speaking from the perspective of the origin, these four were all great sages; just as Śrīmālā was transformed and gained renown for her devotion, it was originally because she was a member of the populace who first wandered in delusion and later attained awakening—a pattern that is but natural within the principles of the path of transformation.
Speaking now from the perspective of the traces [of the teaching], those who have received transformation and attained the prediction are called "born" among the four types of noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the phrase "although born, they have not yet obtained," although they lack actual birth, one knows that the duration of their transformation will not be long.
"Zhen" means "to arrive at.

Therefore, the omens of entering the Way were manifested in advance; for example, because Subhūti realized that phenomena are equal to emptiness, his title of virtue, "Non-contention" (araṇā), was presented beforehand.

Regarding the statement, "Other sūtras designate these as the ten pāramitās," the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* merely groups the six perfections and the four immeasurables to constitute ten perfections; it does not correspond [to the ten pāramitās] precisely.

Regarding the statement, "Within the *mārga-varga*, each section contains a samādhi": among the seven categories, only the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) belong to wisdom (*prajñā*) and the right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) belong to diligence (*vīrya*); within the remaining five categories, all contain the designation of concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the separate listing of names, one should know that these names are established according to their specific functions; the underlying principle is no different.
As for "first informing the mother," because the father was heterodox while the mother was orthodox, he first informed the mother so that they might together devise a plan for conversion.
If one relies upon its fundamental source, mother and child have known each other from the beginning.

Now, according to the ritual of transformation, when the capacity of the disciple has matured and the response is triggered, the hammer and anvil strike one another so that the vessel of the object may finally be perfected; for this reason, it is called "White."

If one conforms to worldly sentiment, the mother’s compassion should be addressed first; furthermore, as the foundation of benefiting others, compassion likewise takes precedence. Since the father-king has already placed his trust [in you] and is well-acquainted with the affairs of the palace, how could he alone be insufficient to transform?
It is simply because those within the palace were not yet mature that the King also waited for the opportune time.

Being able to transform these two layers [of disciples] and deeply discerning their capacities and principles, he attributed the merit of transformation to the Master, thereby synthesizing the teachings of the past and present.
The *Sūtra* says, “It is like a one-eyed turtle,” which, in terms of the actual matter, merely serves as a metaphor for the difficulty of encountering [the Dharma].

If it were used as a vehicle, since ordinary turtles and fish look with both eyes in opposite directions, and it is said that what is seen by a single eye is not correct, how could such a being—already in the ocean of birth and death and moreover possessed of wrong views—encounter the floating wood of the Buddha-dharma and the aperture of the true reality?
Regarding the term "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is fully explained in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also states:
"They are like parents, a guide, a physician, and a ship," and so forth.
Regarding the "purity of the Dharma-eye" mentioned in the section on the benefits of hearing [the teaching], some say it refers to the first fruit [of the path].
But how could this be so, when the royal consort and the eighty thousand others all uphold this sutra and are destined to become Buddhas, yet those who merely hear it attain only the small fruits?
The names may be identical while the meanings differ; this must be carefully considered, as has already been stated previously.
The commentator also says, "that which is seen is pure," and does not say, "the stage of the first fruit of the Hīnayāna."

Explanation of the Chapter on Samantabhadra: Regarding the three aspects of "completeness" (*siddhi*)—first, the world; second, for the sake of others, as in the passage beginning with "Compassionate Flower" (*Karunāpuṣpa*); and third, as an antidote, as in the passage beginning with "I practice"—if one is named according to excelling all others, this is called "Excellence," and thus he is named Samantabhadra.

Regarding the passage from "namely the three *siddhis*" to "the explanation," since the meaning of making vows through the translation of names corresponds to the three *siddhis*, it is stated that they are "furthermore" and "also" the practice of vows.

The phrase "Furthermore, the practices and vows" below also refers back to the three *siddhāntas*, indicating that all three are simultaneously practices and vows; this is how the three *siddhāntas* are used to define practices and vows.

As for the reason why the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate truth) was not established [here]: because the explanation of the "worthy" (*bhadra*) yielded precedence to the "sage" (*ārya*), it is only then that it is named the *paramārtha*. Therefore, in the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the vows encompass the practices, and my practices encompass the vows.
Regarding the phrase "from the beginning," this next section concerns the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*).
It is divided into four parts;
first, the ancient masters' explanations and judgments that it belongs to the *Tripiṭaka*.
"From of old" means "originating from. This refers to the fact that ancient scholars have traditionally offered this interpretation.

Since the name Samantabhadra has a universal application yet distinct meanings, it should also be said to encompass both the universal and the particular; its absence from the text is merely an abbreviation. Thus, we know that the interpretations of Samantabhadra according to the three teachings are all erroneous.
Next, from "Now, to clarify" onwards, the explanation proceeds from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
Third, from "If [one attains] the ten stages of faith" onwards, it further correlates with the preceding stages, moreover refuting both the Common and Distinct Teachings.
Fourth, from "The present treatise" onwards, there is a re-explanation.
Question:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
“Samantabhadra Bodhisattva relies upon suchness (tathatā) and does not rely upon Buddha-lands. Why, then, is it said here that he comes from the East?

Answer: This [text] is based on the traces (nirmāṇakāya) from which he proceeds; that [text] clarifies the essential nature of what has been realized. Since it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi), there still remains a portion of his body within the reward land (saṃbhogakāya).

The sutra follows the ultimate principle; from the very first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one realizes a portion of *tathatā* (suchness), which precisely accords with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Therefore, it subdues the common [vehicles] and severs the partial [paths]; only when the severance of the ultimate is fully subdued is one named Samantabhadra.

Because subduing (the afflictions) begins at the first stage, it is called the "commencement of subduing. Since this refers to a worthy one rather than a universal one, it is "neither the summit nor universal.

Thus, "adjoining the first" refers below to the stage of the first dwelling; as it is the beginning of the ten dwellings, it is not the final culmination. Since the ten grounds merely sever forty grades and do not represent the ultimate limit of severance and subduing, we know that this is not the meaning of Samantabhadra.

The fourfold analysis by way of stages constitutes the formal judgment: first, the formal judgment itself; second, the citation of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (*Śāstra*) to prove its ultimate perfection, which includes the passage from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* cited therein.
Regarding the phrase "possessing the four *siddhāntas*," etc., it was not listed in advance; rather, those very four passages are what is meant.
As for "following [them] away" and so forth, "going" and "moving" merely signify coming and going.
"Following" means that it is not a case of first accumulating and then raining, nor of first storing and then playing; therefore, it is compared to the rain of a dragon.
This is brought about by the power of the mind, the power of the Dharma, the power of sentient beings, the power of responsive transformation, and the power of the inconceivable.

Regarding the phrase "briefly employing two powers": the majestic power and supernormal faculties have already been enumerated in full above; the four qualities, such as mastery (*vaśitā*) and so forth, serve to represent the four virtues.
Now, they are abbreviated to two—omitting mastery and renown—because each of these two [remaining powers] encompasses two [of the original four].
Since the sutra text states that "they, together with countless others, each manifest two powers," one should know that those who are followed are all the Dharma-body.
Because both the principal and the associates possess the four virtues, it says "each."
Since this text appears at the conclusion of the *liutong* (circulation) section, the request to "hear" it implies a dual petition for both the *zhengzong* (main teaching) and the *liutong*.
Within the four lines of text that follow, there are two interpretations: one regarding the *zhengzong* and the other regarding the *liutong*.
The first [section] also has two parts: namely, the trace and the source.
The trace further has two parts:
first, in terms of revealing the real by opening the provisional; second, in terms of opening, showing, awakening, and entering.

In the first section, the first phrase refers to the *dharmakāya*; the second and third refer to *prajñā*; and the fourth refers to *vimukti*. These latter three virtues adorn the *dharmakāya*, and therefore they are related to the first phrase.
In the first sentence, the eight characters from "遠離惡" (distant from evil) onward constitute the four *siddhāntas*.

Next, regarding the interchanging of the four phrases of the scriptures within the context of the "opening" (*kai*) and so forth, this is because they follow the sequential order of the opening and the rest.

Regarding the phrase "only three and only four": the "four" refers simply to the four modes of peaceful conduct (*catur-āśvāsa-pratipatti*); the "three" refers simply to the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and the three [factors] of seat, robe, and dwelling.
In the preceding text, the explanation of the three factors such as the robe applied both to the two phrases, each having both the subject (the agent) and the object;

now, from one perspective, the empty seat is taken as *prajñā*, that which is covered as the *dharmakāya*, and that which covers as *vimukti*. Herein, right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) is included within the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; whereas previously, in the context of the "opening and revealing," right concentration was included within *prajñā*, because this single phrase and those two phrases are established by their respective names.

Regarding the phrase "to give rise to other interpretations": if someone were to reject this interpretation, they would be rejecting one's own practice and the transformation of others; they would be rejecting the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering; they would be rejecting the three—room, clothing, and seat; and they would be rejecting the proper methods for propagating the sutra.

If you say that it is not the case that [the Buddha] did not permit [this], but merely that there is no textual record, then if you claim the sūtra lacks such a record, this implies he did not permit it; yet, since it was necessary to repeat it, why would he have done so? If this were not the case, on what basis could one take the main body of the present sūtra up to this point as a repetition?

At the beginning of the sutra, the four phrases starting with "opening" (kai) were preserved and explained through four interpretations; now, reaching the end of this sutra, it is shown once again that these four phrases starting with "opening" must likewise be interpreted through four explanations. Thus, we know that from beginning to end, these constitute the essence, doctrine, and function of this sutra.
Thus, the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination are none other than the wondrous Dharma.
Regarding what is called the "three cycles" within the teachings of this Dharma, it refers to the recitation and contemplation performed over twenty-one days.
Someone who has reached this point also cites a text stating:

"There are five types of practitioners: first, those with seven lifetimes remaining; second, those with fourteen lifetimes remaining; third, those with one lifetime remaining; fourth, those with two lifetimes remaining; and fifth, those with three lifetimes remaining."
It is further stated that there should be six practices:

first, adorning the ritual site; second, purifying the body; third, the six periods of the day; fourth, making formal invocations; fifth, reciting and chanting; and sixth, contemplating the profound dharma of emptiness.
When one performs this contemplation, one can extinguish hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* heavy offenses.
If that is so, why does this sutra nowhere provide a basis for opening the mind or directing one's thoughts, yet at this point it cites the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra*?

How much more so now, when you yourself have declared: "To those who read, recite, copy, and wish to practice this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, if they apply themselves with single-minded diligence for twenty-one days, I shall mount my elephant and go before them. Therefore, one should know that whether it be practicing or explaining, one must rely upon our present Master to reach the ultimate goal.

Therefore, without the *Xuanwen*, there would be no means to guide; without the *Zhiguan*, there would be no means to attain realization; without this commentary, there would be no means to uphold [the teachings]; and without this school, there would be no means to advance.
If this were not so, what would be the purpose of these teachings?
What would be the point of expounding them?

Therefore, when the nun Huiren of An Guo Temple in the Eastern Capital established a Lotus Sūtra practice hall, those throughout the world today have emulated her; yet they are deluded regarding the source, failing to realize that this nun relied upon a specific foundation and thus personally experienced the response of Samantabhadra.
Nevertheless, although there are those who establish sites for the *dharma-cakra*, they mostly follow their own private opinions.
Furthermore, that current lecturers wish to treat this teaching with negligence stems precisely from their ignorance of its fundamental purport.

Recently, while traveling with over forty monks from the Yangtze and Huai River regions to pay homage at Mount Tai, I encountered Han-guang, a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, who was there by imperial decree overseeing construction projects. He stated that he had personally traveled to India together with the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra.
A monk there asked him:

"In the Great Tang, there exists the legacy of the Tiantai teachings, which is most capable of distinguishing the heterodox from the orthodox and clarifying the partial from the perfect. Would you be able to translate them and bring them to this land?"
Is it not the case that when the Middle Kingdom lost the Dharma, they sought it in the four directions?
Yet, those in this land who possess even a modicum of discernment are as rare as the people of Lu.
Therefore, those of profound virtue who turn toward the Way do not fail to look up to him with reverence.

I respectfully wish that students and practitioners will praise this according to their capacity. It should be understood that this practice for oneself while simultaneously benefiting others differs from other scriptures; whether one speaks or listens, the objective realm and wisdom remain present, and whether the results are latent or manifest, the ripening of the seeds may be expected—all because the propagator of the sutra employs skillful means.
If one were merely to lecture and explain [the sutras] as a propagator of the scriptures, why would there be the need for the three admonitions regarding robes, seats, and dwellings?
How could that which was dispatched by the Tathāgata be treated with such casualness?

As I examine myself and reflect upon my own views, I am personally filled with shame; yet, compelled by various circumstances, I have again ventured to draft this commentary. Although I may establish or refute positions to uphold the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*), it is intended to enable those of like mind to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is ultimately free from partiality and does not follow mere arbitrary conjecture; I hope that all who read this will fully discern my humble sincerity.

A single phrase that colors the spirit provides aid for reaching the other shore; contemplation and cultivation serve forever as a vessel and a sail. Rejoicing in seeing or hearing it, it constantly acts as the primary and its companions; whether grasped or discarded, once it passes through the ears it becomes a condition. Whether favorable or adverse, one ultimately attains liberation thereby. May the day of my liberation see the primary and secondary retributions constantly proclaiming this wondrous sutra; may not a single land or a single speck of dust fail to benefit sentient beings. I only pray that all Buddhas will secretly permeate and bestow their protection, and that all Bodhisattvas will secretly lend their majestic power. Wherever it has not yet been preached, I shall everywhere entreat and request it; wherever it is preached, I shall personally receive and make offerings to it. With every phrase and every verse, may I advance toward Bodhi; with every form and every fragrance, may I never again regress.
The Record of the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Ten, Part Two.
